t: Minimum Swaps To Make Sequences Increasing — Editorial
o: We may swap nums1[i] with nums2[i] at any index, and we want both arrays strictly increasing using the fewest swaps. At each index there are only two states: swapped or not swapped. For Example 1 ([1,3,5,4]/[1,2,3,7]), keeping indices 0-2 as-is is fine; at index 3 the pair (4,7) must be swapped to (7,4) so nums1 ends ...5,7 and nums2 ...3,4 — one swap. For Example 2, swapping index 1 gives [0,1,4,8,9]/[2,3,5,6,9]... actually only one swap (index 1) suffices: [0,1,4,8,9] and [2,3,5,6,9]. Since n can be 10^5, trying all 2^n swap combinations is impossible; we need a per-index DP where each state depends only on the previous index's state.
k: Each index has exactly two choices (swap or not), so a DP over {not-swapped, swapped} states suffices.
A swap at i is valid only if it keeps both sequences increasing relative to index i-1's chosen state.
The four validity conditions come from comparing nums1[i], nums2[i] against nums1[i-1], nums2[i-1]; if neither condition holds for a transition, that path is dead.

a.i: Try every combination of swaps via recursion: at each index decide to swap or not, check strict increase against the previous elements, and take the minimum swaps over all valid paths. This directly models the problem but explores 2^n paths.
s: Recursively process index i carrying the previous values of nums1[i-1] and nums2[i-1] and swaps used so far.
At each index branch into 'no swap' and 'swap', pruning branches where the pair violates strict increase.
Return minimum swaps when reaching the end.
Memoize on (i, prev1, prev2) or just accept exponential time for illustration.
a.t: O(n) states after memoization in theory, but the naive version without memoization is O(2^n); with memoization each of O(n) reachable states costs O(1).
a.sp: O(n) recursion depth plus memo table.

a.n: Approach 2: Optimal DP with Two States (Keep / Swap)
a.i: Track two rolling values: keep[i] = min swaps so both arrays are increasing through index i with no swap at i, and swap[i] = min swaps with a swap at i. Transitions depend only on index i-1: if nums1[i] > nums1[i-1] and nums2[i] > nums2[i-1], we can extend the same choice; if nums1[i] > nums2[i-1] and nums2[i] > nums1[i-1], we can flip the previous choice. One of these conditions always holds because a solution exists.
s: For each i >= 1, start new values at infinity.
If nums1[i] > nums1[i-1] and nums2[i] > nums2[i-1]: newKeep = min(newKeep, keep), newSwap = min(newSwap, swap + 1).
If nums1[i] > nums2[i-1] and nums2[i] > nums1[i-1]: newKeep = min(newKeep, swap), newSwap = min(newSwap, keep + 1).
Answer is min(keep[n-1], swap[n-1]); use O(1) rolling variables instead of arrays.
a.t: O(n) — single pass with constant work per index.
a.sp: O(1) — only two rolling variables per array.

w: In an interview, go straight to the two-state DP after noting the brute force is exponential; explain the four transition conditions carefully since they encode all valid continuations. Common pitfalls: forgetting the 'flip previous choice' transitions (conditions comparing nums1[i] vs nums2[i-1]), initializing swap[0] to 1 rather than 0, and using non-strict comparisons (must be strictly greater). Edge cases: n = 2, arrays already sorted (answer 0), and cases where swapping is forced at every index. Follow-ups: reconstruct which indices were swapped (store parent pointers), or handle the variant where only one array needs to be increasing.
